summary: Describes an RTP header extension that lets a conference mixer tell receivers how loud each participant is. The levels travel in the same RTP packets as the audio, so a client can show who is speaking.

plainLanguage.summary: In a group call, a mixer blends everybody's voices. This lets it also tell each listener who is talking and how loudly, which helps apps highlight the speaker.

questions: rtp mixer to client audio level
what is rtp csrc audio level
how does a mixer report speaker volume in rtp
subtitle: How a conference mixer tells each listener how loud every participant is, inside the audio packets themselves.

tldr.problem: In a mixer-based conference everyone receives one flat audio stream, so clients cannot tell who is speaking or who is making background noise. The CSRC list only gives an on/off hint.
tldr.mechanism: The mixer adds an RTP header extension holding one audio level byte per contributing source, in the same order as the CSRC list. Levels are in -dBov, from 0 to 127.
tldr.outcome: Clients can show a level meter next to every participant, for example to spot who is typing or breathing loudly. The extension is negotiated in SDP and is not encrypted by SRTP.

today: RFC 6465 is a Proposed Standard and the metadata lists no RFC that obsoletes or updates it. It is the companion of RFC 6464, which covers the client-to-mixer direction.

sections.title: Why Listeners Need Levels
sections.content:
In a centralized conference, a mixer combines the media streams of all participants and sends each participant one flat stream. That keeps clients simple, but it makes it hard to tell where a sound comes from.

RTP already lets a mixer list the contributing sources in the CSRC field, but that only says speaking or silent. RFC 6465 adds more detail so a client can notice background chat, music, typing or someone breathing noisily into a microphone, and can even tell a mute participant from one who sends noise. The document describes a user interface where each participant gets a level bar.

The extension is complementary to the one in RFC 6464, which lets clients tell mixers the level of the audio they send.
sections.plainLanguage: Imagine a teacher mixing everyone's shouting into one loudspeaker. You cannot tell who is loud. This adds a little loudness tag per kid so you can see who it is.

sections.title: How the Mixer Reports Levels
sections.content:
The extension uses the general RTP header extension mechanism of RFC 5285. Each instance carries a list of one-octet audio levels. Every value belongs to the CSRC identifier at the same position in the CSRC list, so the number and order of values MUST match the CSRC IDs in the same packet.

A mixer SHOULD report levels for the audio carried in that same packet, and SHOULD calculate them after any processing such as level normalization or noise reduction.

When a conference uses more than one mixer, each mixer MAY relay the CSRC list and levels it gets from peer mixers, as long as the total CSRC count stays below 16. Because the maximum level is not precisely defined, average levels behind different mixers may sound perceptibly different.
sections.plainLanguage: The loudness tags come in the same order as the list of speakers, so the first tag belongs to the first speaker. If there are several mixers, they can pass the lists along.

sections.title: The Audio Level Encoding
sections.content:
The extension element can use either the one-byte or the two-byte header of RFC 5285. In the one-byte form the 4-bit len field is the number of levels minus one, so zero means one byte of data follows. In the two-byte form the 8-bit len field is the exact number of levels. Implementations MUST NOT include more than 15 level values, because RFC 3550 allows at most 15 CSRC IDs. The largest len is therefore 14 for the one-byte form and 15 for the two-byte form.

Each level occupies one byte. The seven least significant bits hold the magnitude, and the most significant bit is unused and always 0. The value is in -dBov, with 0 to 127 meaning 0 to -127 dBov, measured relative to the overload point of the system. Digital silence, such as a muted source, MUST be sent as 127.

The level describes only the audio in that packet, with no long-term averaging or smoothing, and is measured as a root mean square of all samples in the measured range. It is defined the same way as the noise level byte in the comfort noise payload of RFC 3389.
sections.plainLanguage: Loudness is a number from 0 to 127 where 0 is as loud as the system can go and 127 is dead silent. A muted person always shows 127.

sections.title: Negotiating the Extension in SDP
sections.content:
The extension is declared in an SDP extmap attribute with the URI urn:ietf:params:rtp-hdrext:csrc-audio-level. It has no extension attributes. An example line is a=extmap:7 urn:ietf:params:rtp-hdrext:csrc-audio-level, which means packets carrying the extension use ID 7.

Clients that cannot mix cannot produce levels, so they always include the direction recvonly. Focus entities with mixing capability can omit the direction or use sendrecv in offers. They answer sendonly to a recvonly offer and sendrecv to a sendrecv offer.

The extension is defined only for audio. It MUST NOT be advertised with other media types such as video or text.
sections.plainLanguage: Before the call, the app and the mixer agree in a short note that level tags will be used. A plain listener says it only wants to receive them.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
An attacker who modifies RTP packets could make audio activity from one participant look like it comes from another. Also, the level values are not protected even in a Secure RTP (SRTP) session, which may matter when a participant's activity is confidential. As discussed in an informative reference, an attacker might infer information about the conversation, possibly with phoneme-level resolution.

The RFC says these concerns come from the design of RTP itself and would probably also apply to plain CSRC identifiers. Depending on the scenario, implementors and deployers should consider header extension encryption or a lower-level mechanism such as IPsec.
sections.plainLanguage: The loudness tags are not hidden, so someone snooping could learn who is talking. If that matters, use extra locks on the whole connection.

sections.title: Reference Code and IANA Registration
sections.content:
Appendix A gives a non-normative Java class, AudioLevelCalculator, that turns raw linear PCM samples into a level. It computes the root mean square of the normalized samples, converts it to decibels, and clamps the result between -127 and 0. It is not the only way to do this, and it can easily be ported to other languages.

IANA registered the URI urn:ietf:params:rtp-hdrext:csrc-audio-level in the RTP Compact Header Extensions subregistry, described as mixer-to-client audio level indicators.
sections.plainLanguage: The RFC includes sample code that measures how loud a sound is and turns it into the number. Its name was also written in an official list so nobody else uses it.
